chat.said: Our bike repair workshop turns away about 12 repair jobs a week because both mechanics are fully booked. We want the average wait for a repair under 5 days by the end of March, and we can't spend more than £1,500 a month extra. We could hire a part-time mechanic for about £1,300 a month, open on Sundays, or stop taking e-bike jobs, which take roughly twice as long as ordinary ones. Jo thinks Sunday opening would only spread the same work over more days. The average wait is about 9 days now.

answer.text: Hiring a part-time mechanic is the only option with a chance worked out so far: about 66% (if Olumi's estimates hold) of meeting the wait aim, against under 1% for leaving things as they are. Jo's doubt about Sundays is still untested.

why.text: Olumi's challenge to test: turned-away jobs are not in today's wait figure, so freed capacity could let the queue refill.

If Olumi's estimates hold, about 98% if 'Effect of each extra hours/week on average wait for a repair' is low, about 21% if it is high shows the hire's chance swings widely with the effect of each extra hour.

text.text: Suppose the wait is still above target after the hire. What happened to the turned-away customers, and what did the plan quietly assume about them?

brief: Our bike repair workshop turns away about 12 repair jobs a week because both mechanics are fully booked. We want the average wait for a repair under 5 days by the end of March, and we can't spend more than £1,500 a month extra. We could hire a part-time mechanic for about £1,300 a month, open on Sundays, or stop taking e-bike jobs, which take roughly twice as long as ordinary ones. Jo thinks Sunday opening would only spread the same work over more days. The average wait is about 9 days now.
